newsitem.title: USA: US Senators urge fast action on Chile legislation.
newsitem.headline: US Senators urge fast action on Chile legislation.

text.p: Two influential Republican Senators on Tuesday urged Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott to move forward quickly on legislation that would allow U.S. trade officials to negotiate a free trade deal with Chile.

Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz., chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, and Sen. Phil Gramm, R-Tex., told Lott in a letter that the United States would be the "biggest loser" if Congress failed to enact so-called "fast track" legislation.

"Without 'fast track,' it is unlikely that the U.S. can negotiate any agreements to expand (the North American Free Trade Agreement)," the senators argued. "In this vacuum, others will take the lead in shaping the future course of trade liberalization in South America."
The Senators sent a similar letter to Sen. William Roth, R-Del., chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, which will consider the fast track proposals.

Lawmakers are awaiting proposed legislation to be submitted by the Clinton administration. White House economic policy advisor Robert Kyle told the European Institute on Tuesday that administration officials were continuing to work behind the scenes to put together a proposal that could be supported by both Republicans and Democrats. "We will need both Republican and Democratic votes to pass this," Kyle said.
But Republicans and Democrats are split over the issue of whether labor and environmental issues should be included in trade negotiations.
Lott and other influential Republicans have said they would not support legislation that gives the administration broad authority to negotiate those issues.
Kyle said the administration remains committed to those issues and is quietly trying to work it out with lawmakers before submitting a proposed bill.

Administration officials are also worried that unresolved disputes in agricultural trade could undermine its ability to convince lawmakers to support fast track legislation. Fast track allows U.S. officials to negotiate trade agreements without fear they will later be changed by Congress.

A recent NAFTA panel ruling against U.S. complaints about Canadian duties on dairy and poultry imports and other unresolved agricultural trade disputes could undermine support in the agricultural community for the fast track legislation, officials said.
